subtopics.title: Knowledge distillation
subtopics.body:
Distillation trains a small student model to copy a large teacher model on your task. There are two common forms.

In the simpler form, the teacher labels a large set of inputs, and the student is fine-tuned on those outputs as if they were human labels. This works even with a hosted teacher you can only call through an API, subject to that provider's terms.

In the classic form, the student learns to match the teacher's full probability distribution over possible next tokens, called soft labels. A temperature T above 1 softens the distributions so the student learns which wrong answers the teacher considered nearly right. This needs access to the teacher's logits, the raw scores before they become probabilities.
subtopics.example: An e-commerce company routes 2 million product questions a month to one of 40 departments. A large model does it at 96% accuracy but costs too much at that volume. They have it label 50,000 past questions, check a sample of 500 by hand, and fine-tune a small model on the result. The student reaches 94% at a small fraction of the cost per request, and they keep the large model as a fallback for low-confidence cases.
subtopics.code:
import torch.nn.functional as F

def distillation_loss(student_logits, teacher_logits, labels, T=2.0, alpha=0.5):
    # soft part: match the teacher's softened distribution
    soft = F.kl_div(
        F.log_softmax(student_logits / T, dim=-1),
        F.softmax(teacher_logits / T, dim=-1),
        reduction="batchmean",
    ) * (T * T)                                   # rescale so gradients stay comparable
    # hard part: still learn from the true labels
    hard = F.cross_entropy(student_logits, labels)
    return alpha * soft + (1 - alpha) * hard

glossary: Fine-tuning
Continuing to train a pretrained model on your own examples to change its behaviour.
Weights
The learned numbers inside a model that determine its outputs.
LoRA
Low-rank adaptation: training two small matrices that add a correction to frozen weights.
Rank (r)
The inner size of LoRA's two small matrices, which controls how many parameters the adapter has.
Adapter
The saved LoRA weights, a small file loaded on top of the base model.
Quantization
Storing numbers with fewer bits, such as 4 instead of 16, to save memory.
QLoRA
LoRA training on a base model loaded in 4-bit precision.
Distillation
Training a small student model to imitate the outputs of a larger teacher model.
Soft labels
The teacher's full probability distribution over answers, used as a training target.
Catastrophic forgetting
When training on a new task makes a model worse at things it could do before.
practice: Run the small LoRA arithmetic example in plain PyTorch and change d and r. Make a table of trainable parameter counts for r = 4, 16 and 64.

Using PEFT, attach a LoRA config to a small open model (for example one under 1B parameters) and call print_trainable_parameters(). Then prepare a 200-example JSONL dataset for a narrow task, such as classifying support tickets into 5 categories, with a 50-example held-out test set.

Stretch: fine-tune that small model with SFTTrainer on a free or rented GPU, report accuracy on the test set before and after tuning, and write a half-page note explaining whether RAG or a better prompt could have achieved the same result.

evals.plain: An eval (short for evaluation) is a repeatable test that measures how well an AI system does its job. You collect a set of realistic inputs, run them through the system, and score the outputs automatically where you can and with people where you must. Because language model outputs vary and are hard to check with a simple equals sign, evals combine exact code checks, a second model acting as a judge, and human review. The result is a score you can compare between versions before you ship a change.
evals.analogy: Evals are like the tasting panel in a food factory. Before a new recipe goes out, the same set of testers tastes the same dishes, scores them on the same checklist, and the recipe only ships if it scores at least as well as the old one.
evals.why: Customers will not trust an AI system because a demo looked good. An FDE needs numbers that show the system works on the customer's real cases, and that a new prompt or model did not break anything. When a bank asks "how do we know the assistant is accurate enough for our advisors?", the eval set is the answer.

subtopics.title: Building a golden dataset
subtopics.body:
A golden dataset is a fixed set of test cases with known good answers or clear grading notes. It is the foundation of every other step.

Take cases from real usage: past tickets, real questions, real documents. Invented examples tend to be easier than real ones. Include the hard cases users complain about, and some cases where the correct behaviour is to refuse or say "I don't know".

Tag each case with slices, meaning categories you will report separately, such as topic, language or customer type. Start with 50 to 200 cases. It is better to have 100 good cases this week than 2,000 next quarter.
subtopics.example: A wealth management firm wants an assistant for advisors. You collect 150 real questions from their internal help channel over 3 months. A senior advisor writes the expected answer or key facts for each. You tag them by slice: 60 product rules, 40 tax, 30 account operations, 20 that must be refused because they require personal advice. You store them in a versioned JSONL file.

subtopics.title: Code-based checks first
subtopics.body:
Start with checks that code can do exactly and cheaply. Does the output parse as valid JSON? Does it match the required schema? Does a generated SQL query run? Is every cited source id real? Is the answer under the length limit? Does it contain a required fact?

These checks are deterministic, so they never disagree with themselves, and they run in milliseconds.

They do not judge quality in general, but they catch a surprising share of real failures. Run them first, and only send outputs that pass to the slower, more expensive checks.
subtopics.example: For the advisor assistant, three code checks run on each answer: it cites at least one source id that exists in the index, it contains every string in must_include, and for refuse cases it contains none of the words buy, sell or hold as advice. On the first run, 11 of 150 answers fail the citation check because the model invented a document id. That bug would have been hard to spot by reading answers.
subtopics.code:
import json

VALID_SOURCES = set(json.load(open("index_source_ids.json")))

def code_checks(case, answer, cited_ids):
    results = {}
    results["cites_real_source"] = bool(cited_ids) and set(cited_ids) <= VALID_SOURCES
    results["has_required_facts"] = all(s.lower() in answer.lower()
                                        for s in case["must_include"])
    if case["slice"] == "refuse":
        banned = ["you should buy", "you should sell", "i recommend"]
        results["refused_properly"] = not any(b in answer.lower() for b in banned)
    results["length_ok"] = len(answer.split()) <= 250
    return results

print(code_checks({"slice": "tax", "must_include": ["taxable"]},
                  "Yes, the converted amount is taxable [S14].", ["S14"]))

subtopics.title: LLM-as-judge with a rubric
subtopics.body:
Some qualities need judgement: is the answer correct, complete, and helpful? A common method is to ask a strong model to grade the output against a written rubric. This is called LLM-as-judge.

Write the rubric like instructions to a new human grader. Define each score level with concrete criteria. Give the judge the question, the reference answer or grading notes, and the system's answer. Ask for a short reason before the score, and ask for a fixed output format so your code can read it.

Judges have biases. They may favour longer answers or their own writing style. Use a narrow scale such as pass or fail, or 1 to 5, and grade one quality at a time.
subtopics.example: The advisor assistant's correctness judge uses a 1 to 5 scale. A score of 5 means all key facts from the grading notes are present and nothing is wrong. A score of 3 means partly correct with a missing fact. A score of 1 means a materially wrong statement. For q002, the answer says Roth conversions are taxable but forgets to mention the tax desk, and the judge gives 4 with that reason.
subtopics.code:
import anthropic, json
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

RUBRIC = """Grade the ANSWER for correctness against the GRADING NOTES.
5 = all key facts present, nothing incorrect
4 = correct but misses a minor point from the notes
3 = partly correct, misses a key fact
2 = mostly incorrect or misleading
1 = contains a materially wrong statement
Reply as JSON: {"reason": "<one sentence>", "score": <1-5>}"""

def judge(case, answer):
    msg = (f"{RUBRIC}\n\nQUESTION: {case['question']}\n"
           f"GRADING NOTES: {case['grading_notes']}\nANSWER: {answer}")
    resp = client.messages.create(model=JUDGE_MODEL, max_tokens=200,
                                  messages=[{"role": "user", "content": msg}])
    return json.loads(resp.content[0].text)

subtopics.title: Calibrating the judge against humans
subtopics.body:
An uncalibrated judge is only an opinion. Before you trust it, compare it with humans.

Have one or two domain experts score a sample of 50 to 100 outputs with the same rubric, without seeing the judge's scores. Then measure agreement. Simple percent agreement is a start. Cohen's kappa is better, because it corrects for agreement that would happen by chance. As a rough guide, higher kappa means stronger agreement, and values near zero mean the judge is no better than chance.

Read the disagreements. Usually the rubric is unclear on some point. Tighten it and re-measure. Repeat periodically, because models and data change.
subtopics.example: An advisor grades 80 answers as pass or fail. The judge agrees on 64 of 80, which is 80%, and kappa is 0.52. Reading the 16 disagreements shows the judge passes answers that omit the tax desk caveat. You add "missing the tax desk caveat on tax questions is a fail" to the rubric. On a fresh sample, agreement rises to 92% and kappa to 0.81.
subtopics.code:
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score, confusion_matrix

human = ["pass","fail","pass","pass","fail","pass","fail","pass","pass","fail"]
judge = ["pass","pass","pass","pass","fail","pass","fail","pass","fail","fail"]

agree = sum(h == j for h, j in zip(human, judge)) / len(human)
kappa = cohen_kappa_score(human, judge)            # corrects for chance agreement

print(f"agreement {agree:.0%}, kappa {kappa:.2f}")
print(confusion_matrix(human, judge, labels=["pass", "fail"]))
# rows = human label, columns = judge label; read the off-diagonal cases

subtopics.title: Reporting by slice and comparing versions
subtopics.body:
A single overall score hides problems. Report scores per slice, and compare each slice between the current version and the candidate.

A version is everything that affects output: the prompt, the model, retrieval settings, tools and code. Record the version id with every eval run.

With small datasets, differences of a few points can be noise. Look at which individual cases flipped from pass to fail and read them. For important decisions, rerun a few times, since model outputs vary.
subtopics.example: The team tries a new prompt. Overall pass rate goes from 84% to 87%, which looks like a win. By slice: product rules up from 80% to 90%, tax flat at 85%, account operations flat, but refuse down from 95% to 75%. Four cases that used to decline personal advice now give it. The change is blocked and the refusal instructions are restored.
subtopics.code:
import pandas as pd

# one row per (version, case) with a pass/fail result
df = pd.read_csv("eval_results.csv")   # columns: version, case_id, slice, passed

by_slice = (df.groupby(["slice", "version"])["passed"].mean()
              .unstack("version").round(2))
by_slice["delta"] = by_slice["v2"] - by_slice["v1"]
print(by_slice.sort_values("delta"))    # worst regressions first

flipped = df.pivot(index="case_id", columns="version", values="passed")
print(flipped[(flipped["v1"] == 1) & (flipped["v2"] == 0)].index.tolist())

subtopics.title: Gating releases and learning from production
subtopics.body:
Offline evals run on a fixed dataset. Put them in CI (continuous integration, the automated checks that run on every code change) so every prompt or model change is tested before merge. Set thresholds per slice, agreed with the customer, and fail the build when a key slice drops.

Online signals come from real use: thumbs up and down, whether users copy the answer, escalations to a human, A/B tests. They show whether the system creates value, which offline evals cannot fully show.

Close the loop. Every production failure that someone reports becomes a new case in the golden set, after an expert writes the expected answer. The dataset grows with the customer's real usage.
subtopics.example: The bank agrees thresholds with the head of advisory: refuse slice at least 95%, every other slice at least 85%. The CI job fails if any slice misses. In the first month in production, advisors thumbs-down 42 answers. Reviewing them yields 25 new eval cases, mostly about a new product launched after the index was built, which also reveals that re-indexing was not scheduled.

glossary: Eval
A repeatable test that scores an AI system's outputs on a fixed set of cases.
Golden dataset
A curated set of real test cases with expected answers or grading notes.
Slice
A subset of cases, such as a topic or customer type, reported separately.
LLM-as-judge
Using a language model with a written rubric to grade another system's outputs.
Rubric
Written criteria that define what each score means.
Calibration
Checking and adjusting a judge until its scores agree with expert human scores.
Cohen's kappa
An agreement measure between two graders that corrects for agreement expected by chance.
Regression
A drop in quality on cases that previously worked.
CI gate
An automated check that blocks a change from merging if it fails set thresholds.
Online signal
A measure from real usage, such as user feedback or escalations.
practice: Pick any LLM feature you have built or can build in an hour (for example, summarizing support tickets). Write 30 test cases in JSONL with slices and grading notes, including 5 cases where the right answer is to decline.
Write code checks and an LLM judge with a 1 to 5 rubric. Grade 20 outputs by hand yourself, compute percent agreement and Cohen's kappa with the judge, and revise the rubric once.

Stretch: create two versions of your prompt, run both through the full eval, produce a per-slice comparison table and a list of flipped cases, and wire a script into a GitHub Actions workflow that fails when any slice drops below its threshold.

case.plain: Case decomposition is the skill of breaking a vague business request into clear, answerable parts before designing anything. In an FDE interview, the case round gives you a prompt like "a hospital wants to use AI to reduce discharge delays" and watches how you think. You clarify the goal, find the users and the sponsor (the person who pays), map how the work happens today, check what data exists, choose a success metric, name the constraints, and propose a small first step. The same method is how real customer engagements start.
case.analogy: It is like a doctor seeing a new patient who says "I feel unwell". A good doctor asks questions, examines, and orders a test before prescribing anything, and starts with the treatment that is safest and most likely to help.
case.why: Customers rarely arrive with a precise problem. They arrive with a goal, a budget and a hunch about AI. An FDE who jumps straight to architecture builds the wrong thing. An FDE who decomposes the case finds the real bottleneck, sets a metric the sponsor cares about, and ships something small that proves value within weeks.

subtopics.title: Restate and clarify the goal
subtopics.body:
Start by saying the problem back in your own words and asking what "better" means. This shows you listen, and it often reveals that the stated ask is a guess at a solution.

Ask a few clarifying questions: Why now? What happens if nothing changes? How do they measure the problem today? Which part of the organisation is involved?

Do not propose any technology yet. Interviewers watch for candidates who design too early. Customers do too.
subtopics.example: Prompt: "A regional hospital wants AI to reduce discharge delays." You restate: "So the goal is to shorten the time between a patient being medically ready to leave and actually leaving, which frees beds. Is that right, and is this across all wards or specific ones?" The interviewer says the COO is worried because the emergency department is boarding patients who wait for beds. Now you know the real driver is bed capacity.
subtopics.code:
Clarifying questions template

Goal        : What outcome would make this a success in 6 months?
Why now     : What changed? What does the problem cost today?
Scope       : Which sites, teams, products or wards?
Measure     : How is the problem measured now, if at all?
Sponsor     : Who asked for this, and who approves the budget?
Tried before: What has been tried, and why did it not work?

subtopics.title: Users, sponsor and stakeholders
subtopics.body:
Separate three groups. Users do the daily work and would use the tool. The sponsor funds the project and cares about a business result. Other stakeholders can block or slow you: IT, security, legal, compliance, unions.

Each group wants something different. The COO wants beds. Nurses want less paperwork. IT wants nothing that breaks the EHR (electronic health record, the hospital's main patient system).

A solution that pleases the sponsor but adds work for users will not be adopted. Say this tension out loud in the interview.
subtopics.example: At the hospital, users are case managers, charge nurses, physicians and pharmacists. The sponsor is the COO. Stakeholders include the CIO (owns the EHR), the privacy officer (patient data), and the nursing union (workload). You note that case managers already spend about 2 hours a day chasing status by phone, so a tool that saves them time has a natural path to adoption.
subtopics.code:
| Group         | Who                      | Wants                        | Risk if ignored        |
|---------------|--------------------------|------------------------------|------------------------|
| Sponsor       | COO                      | More beds, less ED boarding  | Funding stops          |
| Users         | Case managers, nurses    | Less chasing, fewer calls    | Tool is not used       |
| Users         | Physicians               | No extra clicks              | Orders stay late       |
| Gatekeeper    | CIO / EHR team           | No EHR instability           | No data access         |
| Gatekeeper    | Privacy officer          | HIPAA compliance, audit logs | Project blocked        |

subtopics.title: Map the current workflow
subtopics.body:
Draw the steps of the process as it works today, including handoffs between people and systems. A handoff is where work passes from one person or team to another. Delays usually hide at handoffs.

For each step, ask who does it, which system they use, and how long it takes. Ask for the typical case and the slow case.

Find the bottleneck: the single step that accounts for most of the delay. Improving any other step barely changes the total.
subtopics.example: Discharge today: physician writes the discharge order (often after morning rounds, around 11:00), pharmacy reconciles medications, nurse does patient education, transport is booked, family is called for pickup. Timing data from one ward shows medication reconciliation takes a median of 2.5 hours because pharmacy only learns about a discharge once the order is signed. That is the bottleneck.
subtopics.code:
-- Where does the time go? Median minutes per discharge step, last 90 days
SELECT step_name,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY minutes) AS median_min,
       PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY minutes) AS p90_min,
       COUNT(*) AS discharges
FROM (
  SELECT e.encounter_id, e.step_name,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (e.completed_at - e.started_at)) / 60 AS minutes
  FROM   discharge_events e
  WHERE  e.ward = '4 West'
    AND  e.started_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'
) t
GROUP BY step_name
ORDER BY median_min DESC;

subtopics.title: Data reality and constraints
subtopics.body:
Ask what data exists, where it lives, how fresh it is, and who can grant access. Much important information sits in free-text notes, spreadsheets or whiteboards, and some is not recorded at all.

Data access is often the slowest part of a real project. Start the access request on day one.

Then list constraints before you design: privacy law (HIPAA for US health data), where the system must run (on-premises, the customer's cloud account, or a vendor cloud), required humans in the loop, integration limits, budget and timeline. Constraints narrow the design space and show the interviewer you have done this before.
subtopics.example: Discharge orders and medication lists are in the EHR and available through a read-only reporting database refreshed every 15 minutes. "Likely discharge tomorrow" exists only in physicians' progress notes as free text. Transport bookings are in a separate scheduling tool. Constraints: patient data must stay inside the hospital's cloud account, every AI suggestion must be confirmed by a nurse, and the EHR team will not allow writes into the EHR in the first phase.
subtopics.code:
Data and constraints inventory

Data source             System         Freshness   Access          Notes
Discharge orders        EHR reporting  15 min      Read, via CIO   Structured
Medication lists        EHR reporting  15 min      Read, via CIO   Structured
"Likely d/c tomorrow"   Progress notes Real time   Read, via CIO   Free text only
Transport bookings      Scheduler      Hourly      API key needed  Separate vendor

Constraints
- PHI stays in the hospital's cloud tenant (HIPAA, BAA required)
- Nurse confirms every suggestion; no autonomous actions
- No writes to the EHR in phase 1
- Pilot budget: 8 weeks, 2 engineers

subtopics.title: Success metric, baseline and guardrail
subtopics.body:
Pick one primary metric that the sponsor cares about and that your work can move. Measure its baseline, the value before you change anything. Without a baseline you cannot prove impact.

Add a guardrail metric, which must not get worse. It stops you from "winning" in a harmful way, such as rushing patients out.

If possible, compare the pilot group with a similar control group over the same period. This separates your effect from seasonal changes or other projects.
subtopics.example: Primary metric: median hours from medically ready to discharge on ward 4 West. Baseline over the last 90 days: 6.5 hours. Guardrail: 30-day readmission rate, baseline 11.2%. Control: ward 5 West, similar patient mix. Target agreed with the COO: 1.5 hours saved on the pilot ward within 8 weeks with no rise in readmissions. The small calculation below turns the target into beds, which is the language the sponsor uses.
subtopics.code:
# Translate hours saved into bed capacity for the sponsor
discharges_per_day = 14          # ward 4 West average
hours_saved_each   = 1.5         # target reduction in median delay
bed_hours_per_day  = 24

bed_hours_freed = discharges_per_day * hours_saved_each
beds_equivalent = bed_hours_freed / bed_hours_per_day
print(f"{bed_hours_freed:.0f} bed-hours/day = {beds_equivalent:.2f} beds on one ward")

# Across 10 similar wards if the pilot scales
print(f"Hospital-wide: {beds_equivalent * 10:.1f} beds")

subtopics.title: Thin slice, plan and risks
subtopics.body:
A thin slice is the smallest version that solves one real problem for real users end to end. It is narrow in scope, but it works in production conditions with real data.

Pick the slice at the bottleneck. Describe what users see, what data it uses, and how a human stays in control. Give a short week-by-week plan with a demo point.

Close with the top risks and one mitigation each. Common risks are data access delays, users not trusting the tool, model errors, and scope creep. Then explain how the slice would expand if it works.
subtopics.example: Slice: each evening, a model reads progress notes and orders on 4 West and produces a list of patients likely to be discharged tomorrow. Pharmacy gets the list and starts medication reconciliation early. A charge nurse confirms or removes each name. Weeks 1 to 2: access and baseline. Weeks 3 to 4: build the list and test on past data. Week 5: demo to COO and pharmacy lead. Weeks 6 to 8: live pilot. Risks: data access (mitigation: start the request on day one), nurse trust (show reasons for each prediction), wrong predictions (nurse confirms, and overrides become eval data).
subtopics.code:
8-week pilot plan: Predicted discharge list, ward 4 West

Wk 1-2  Access approved, baseline measured, shadow 3 discharges
Wk 3-4  Build nightly list from notes + orders; backtest on 60 days
        Target: 80% of next-day discharges appear on the list
Wk 5    Demo to COO, pharmacy lead, charge nurses; adjust
Wk 6-8  Live pilot; nurse confirms each name; weekly metric review

Top risks                     Mitigation
Data access slips             Request on day 1; CIO sponsor escalation
Nurses ignore the list        Show the note snippet behind each prediction
Wrong predictions             Human confirms; log overrides as eval cases
Scope creep to other wards    Expansion only after week-8 review

glossary: Case decomposition
Breaking a vague business request into goal, users, workflow, data, metric, constraints and a first step.
Sponsor
The senior person who funds the project and cares about its business result.
Stakeholder
Anyone who is affected by the project or can approve, slow or block it.
Handoff
A point where work passes from one person, team or system to another.
Bottleneck
The step in a process that accounts for most of the total delay.
Baseline
The value of a metric before any change, used to measure impact.
Guardrail metric
A metric that must not get worse while you improve the primary metric.
Thin slice
The smallest end-to-end solution that delivers real value to real users.
EHR
Electronic health record, the main clinical system in a hospital.
Control group
A similar group that does not get the change, used for comparison.
practice: Pick one prompt, such as "An insurer wants AI to speed up claims" or "A retailer wants AI to cut returns". Write the clarifying questions and a stakeholder table (users, sponsor, gatekeepers) in under 15 minutes.
For the same prompt, sketch the current workflow with at least 5 steps and handoffs, choose a primary metric with an assumed baseline and a guardrail metric, and list 4 constraints.

Stretch: do a timed 30-minute mock case out loud with a friend playing the interviewer. Finish with a thin slice, an 8-week plan, and 3 risks with mitigations. Record it, then score yourself on whether you asked questions before designing.
